references.text: Proverbs warns against taking a seat of honor in the presence of nobles, for it is better to be invited up than to be humbled before someone of higher rank. Jesus' parable in Luke 14 directly reflects this wisdom tradition. [ref:Prov 25:6-7|Proverbs 25:6-7]
The immediate context of the verse – Jesus' parable about choosing the lowest seat at the table, with the point that whoever exalts themselves will be humbled. [ref:Lk 14:7-11|Luke 14:7-11]
When pride comes, shame (αἰσχύνη) also comes, which corresponds to the shame (μετὰ αἰσχύνης) described in Luke 14:9 when one is forced to move to the lowest place. [ref:Prov 11:2|Proverbs 11:2]

Pride leads to humiliation, but the humble in spirit gain honor – a wisdom saying that directly corresponds with the theme of shame through self-exaltation in Jesus' parable. [ref:Prov 29:23|Proverbs 29:23]

Jesus repeats the principle that whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted – the same main point as in the parable about table seats. [ref:Lk 18:14|Luke 18:14]
James quotes Proverbs and emphasizes that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble – the same principle behind the shame of being asked to move down. [ref:Jas 4:6|James 4:6]
"Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you" – this corresponds to the positive counterpart in Luke 14:10-11, where whoever takes the lowest seat is honored. [ref:Jas 4:10|James 4:10]

Peter urges humility and quotes the same principle: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Whoever humbles themselves under God's mighty hand will be exalted. [ref:1 Pet 5:5-6|1 Peter 5:5-6]

Jesus states the same principle in Matthew: "Whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted" – identical to the conclusion in [ref:Lk 14:11|Luke 14:11]. [ref:Matt 23:12|Matthew 23:12]
